text: All three dimensions are standing. This video builds the center of the star: fact_sales — wired to dim_date, dim_store, and dim_product with real foreign keys, on the surrogate keys, never the natural ones.

That choice is what makes the Type 2 history on dim_product actually work. A historical sale keeps pointing at whichever product_key was current the day it happened, no matter how many price changes that SKU has gone through since.

We enforce the grain at the database level, not just on a whiteboard — a unique constraint on date_key, store_key, and product_key together. If a bug ever tries to insert the same store-product-day twice, SQL Server rejects it instead of silently doubling that row's sales.

For the index, we skip a traditional rowstore index and use a clustered columnstore index instead. It compresses heavily on a table where store and date repeat constantly, and it's built exactly for the sum-and-group-by queries the report and dashboard both run constantly.

One more constraint ties straight back to the very first video: a check constraint that forces net_sales_amount to always equal gross minus returns minus employee discount. That's Finance's agreed definition, enforced by the database itself, not just assumed correct.

A quick grain check confirms zero duplicate rows, and the grain gets documented directly on the table itself, so any future maintainer can read it from the database rather than trusting a document stays in sync. The core data model is done. Starting next video, the work shifts to actually getting nightly data flowing into it.
